blocks.text: 1. Introduction

You have probably built a pivot table before, even if you have never written a line of pandas. Open a spreadsheet full of sales records, drag region into the Rows box, drag month into the Columns box, drag sale amount into the Values box, and Excel or Google Sheets hands you back a clean summary grid. That exact operation, reshaping a long list of rows into a wide summary table, is what pd.pivot_table does, except now it is one line of code instead of a few clicks and a mouse.

pd.pivot_table() is one of the most useful tools in pandas for turning raw, row by row data into something a human can actually read at a glance. A thousand rows of individual sales transactions is exhausting to scan. A small grid with regions down the side, months across the top, and average sale amounts filling the cells tells you the whole story in one look.

items: A sales report with regions down the side and months across the top.
A grade book with students as rows and subjects as columns.
A budget spreadsheet with expense categories as rows and months as columns.
Any Excel pivot table you have ever built by dragging fields into Rows, Columns, and Values.

blocks.text: Every one of those examples has the same shape underneath. You take long, row based data, and reshape it into a wide grid where one column's unique values become new row labels, another column's unique values become new column headers, and a third column gets aggregated to fill in the cells.

blocks.caption: pivot_table turns long data into a wide summary grid, the same thing an Excel pivot table does.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415810-235599735.png

If you have already worked through the groupby lesson, you are in a great position here. pivot_table leans on the exact same split, apply, combine machinery under the hood that groupby uses. It just arranges the final output differently, as a grid instead of a flat list. This lesson builds directly on that foundation, so keep the groupby mental model close by.
2. The Pivot Table Mental Model

Every pd.pivot_table() call needs the same three ingredients, no matter how complicated it ends up looking. One column supplies the row labels. Another column supplies the column headers. A third column gets aggregated down to a single number that fills in each cell of the resulting grid.

Picture a table of sales records with a region column, a product category column, and a total sale amount column. Turn region into rows, category into columns, and average the total for each combination, and you get a compact grid where every single cell answers one very specific question: what is the average sale for this region and this category.
2.1 Rows: The index Parameter

The index parameter tells pivot_table which column's unique values become the row labels of the result. Pass index="region" and pandas collects every distinct region in your data, North, South, East, and gives each one its own row in the output grid.

blocks.caption: index picks which column's values turn into row labels.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415810-144565126.png
2.2 Columns: The columns Parameter

The columns parameter works exactly the same way, just sideways. Pass columns="category" and every distinct category in your data becomes a column header stretched across the top of the grid, instead of a row running down the side.

blocks.caption: columns picks which column's values turn into column headers.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415810-216825507.png

index and columns are doing the identical job: sorting a column's unique values onto a new axis of the result. The only real difference between them is which direction that axis points once the grid is drawn.
2.3 Values and aggfunc: What Fills Each Cell

values tells pivot_table which column supplies the raw numbers, and aggfunc tells it how to squash however many matching rows down into the single number that lands in each cell. Pass values="total" and aggfunc="mean", and every cell shows the average total for that specific region and category combination.

If you leave aggfunc out entirely, pivot_table quietly defaults to the mean. That is a real difference from groupby, where you always had to name a function explicitly through .mean() or .agg(). Skipping aggfunc here does not raise an error, it just silently averages, so it is worth typing aggfunc="mean" anyway to make your intent obvious to anyone reading the code later, including future you.

blocks.alt: Values and aggfunc: What Fills Each Cell
blocks.caption: values plus aggfunc decide what number lands in each cell.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415811-457795907.png

blocks.title: aggfunc accepts more than a name
blocks.content: You are not limited to string names like "mean" or "sum". aggfunc also accepts an actual function, including one you write yourself, such as aggfunc=lambda x: x.max()-x.min() to get the spread between each cell's largest and smallest value. Anything you could pass into groupby's .agg() works here too.

blocks.text: 3. Your First Pivot Table
Let's make this concrete with the same orders DataFrame from the groupby lesson: seven orders, each tagged with a region, a product category, a total amount spent, and a quantity.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "region":   ["North", "South", "North", "East", "South", "East", "North"],
    "category": ["Electronics", "Clothing", "Clothing", "Electronics", "Electronics", "Clothing", "Electronics"],
    "total":    [250, 80, 120, 300, 150, 60, 400],
    "quantity": [2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 4],
})
orders

blocks.text: Grouping by region and category with groupby gave you a tidy list, one row per combination, with a hierarchical index. pivot_table takes those exact same three columns and lays them out as an actual grid instead.

code.content:
pd.pivot_table(orders, index="region", columns="category", values="total", aggfunc="mean")

# category  Clothing  Electronics
# region
# East          60.0        300.0
# North        120.0        325.0
# South         80.0        150.0

blocks.text: Every one of those numbers should look familiar. They are the exact same averages the groupby version computed: North Electronics at 325.0, East Clothing at 60.0, and so on. pivot_table did not calculate anything new, it just arranged the same answers into a grid instead of a stacked list.
4. Missing Cells: NaN and fill_value

Real data is rarely as tidy as that orders example, where every region sold something in every category. Add a third category, Home, that only shows up in the North and South regions, plus a couple of repeat orders so the aggregation actually has something to average, and you get a genuine gap in the grid.

East never sold anything in the Home category, so there is no row at all for pivot_table to aggregate for that specific region and category combination. Pivot this and watch what happens in the East row under the Home column.

code.content:
pd.pivot_table(orders2, index="region", columns="category", values="total", aggfunc="mean")

# category  Clothing  Electronics  Home
# region
# East          60.0        300.0   NaN
# North        120.0        200.0  90.0
# South         80.0        150.0  60.0

blocks.text: North Electronics landed on 200.0 instead of a single order total, because two separate North Electronics orders, 250 and 150, both fell into that one cell and got averaged together. East and Home, on the other hand, simply never occurred together anywhere in the data. Rather than guessing at a number, pandas fills that gap with NaN, its standard placeholder for missing data.

blocks.caption: A missing region and category combination shows up as NaN unless you tell pivot_table otherwise.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415811-686223054.png

blocks.title: NaN is not the same as zero
blocks.content: Do not assume a NaN cell secretly means zero. It means pandas found no rows at all for that combination. Summing or comparing a column full of NaN values behaves very differently from a column full of real zeros, so decide deliberately whether a gap should count as zero, stay blank, or get handled some other way.

blocks.text: When a gap really does mean zero, for example zero sales rather than some unknown or unmeasured value, the fill_value parameter replaces every one of those NaN cells with whatever you pass in.

code.content:
pd.pivot_table(orders2, index="region", columns="category", values="total", aggfunc="mean", fill_value=0)

# category  Clothing  Electronics  Home
# region
# East          60.0        300.0   0.0
# North        120.0        200.0  90.0
# South         80.0        150.0  60.0

blocks.title: fill_value only patches gaps in the grid
blocks.content: fill_value replaces cells where an entire row and column combination is missing from your source data. It has no effect on genuine null values that were already sitting inside your values column before you ever called pivot_table. Clean those up separately, for example with fillna() on the source DataFrame first, if that is what you actually need.

blocks.text: 5. Multiple Aggregations at Once

Sometimes the mean alone does not tell the whole story. Maybe you want the average total per region and category, and the total revenue, in the very same grid. Pass a list of function names to aggfunc instead of a single string, and pivot_table computes every one of them.

code.content:
pd.pivot_table(orders2, index="region", columns="category", values="total", aggfunc=["mean", "sum"])

#             mean                     sum
# category Clothing Electronics Home  Clothing Electronics Home
# region
# East          60.0        300.0  NaN      60.0        300.0  NaN
# North        120.0        200.0 90.0     120.0        400.0 90.0
# South         80.0        150.0 60.0      80.0        150.0 60.0

blocks.text: The result comes back with an extra level of column headers stacked on top: one full block of columns for mean, sitting right next to a second full block of columns for sum, both using the same category headers underneath. North Electronics shows a mean of 200.0 and a sum of 400.0 side by side, because the two separate orders that landed in that cell get averaged for one block and totaled for the other.

blocks.caption: A list passed to aggfunc produces one stacked block of columns per function.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442416162-416078469.png

blocks.title: values can be a list too
blocks.content: aggfunc is not the only parameter that accepts a list. Pass a list of column names to values as well, such as values=["total", "quantity"], and pivot_table produces one stacked block per value column instead of, or in addition to, one block per aggregation function.

blocks.text: 6. Row and Column Totals with margins

A real report often needs an overall total row and an overall total column, the same Grand Total row and column you get for free at the edge of an Excel pivot table. Set margins=True and pivot_table adds exactly that.

code.content:
pd.pivot_table(orders2, index="region", columns="category", values="total", aggfunc="mean", margins=True)

# category  Clothing  Electronics   Home         All
# region
# East          60.0        300.0    NaN       180.0
# North        120.0        200.0   90.0       152.5
# South         80.0        150.0   60.0   96.666667
# All       86.666667       212.5   75.0       140.0

blocks.text: The new All row shows the overall average total for each category across every region combined. The new All column shows the overall average for each region across every category combined. The single cell where the All row meets the All column, in the bottom right corner, is the grand average across the whole dataset.

blocks.alt: Row and Column Totals with margins
blocks.caption: margins=True adds an All row, an All column, and one grand total cell.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442416164-652918623.png

blocks.title: All is computed from the real data, not the visible grid
blocks.content: East's All value is 180.0, based on East's two actual sales, not some average of the cells you see in that row including the NaN gap under Home. margins always aggregates the underlying rows directly, so a missing combination does not quietly drag a total down or push it up. This also means margins and fill_value never interact in a surprising way: fill_value only changes what a missing cell displays, it does not change what the All totals get computed from.

blocks.text: You can rename that row and column away from the default label All with the margins_name parameter, for example margins_name="Total", if that label reads better for whoever ends up looking at the final report.
7. pivot_table Is Really groupby Plus unstack

Here is the part that ties this whole lesson back to the last one. pivot_table is not a separate engine doing something fundamentally new. It is syntactic sugar over a groupby call followed by an unstack, wrapped up into a single convenient function.
Take the plain orders example from earlier and run both versions side by side.
Both produce the exact same grid.

groupby(["region", "category"]) does the split, matching pivot_table's index plus columns. .mean() does the apply, matching pivot_table's values plus aggfunc. .unstack("category") does the final reshaping step, lifting category out of the row index and laying it across the top as column headers, which is exactly the shape pivot_table hands you back directly, in one call.

blocks.alt: pivot_table Is Really groupby Plus unstack
blocks.caption: pivot_table is groupby, an aggregation, and unstack, bundled into one call.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442416164-680799769.png

blocks.title: So when should you reach for which
blocks.content: Reach for pivot_table when you know up front that you want a grid shaped report, especially with multiple aggregation functions or margins, since it gets you there in one readable line. Reach for groupby directly when you want a flat, list shaped result, or when your next step is something unstack cannot easily express, like a custom per group function.

blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: A Region by Month Sales Report

Let's put everything from this lesson together and build a report you would genuinely hand to someone: sales data reshaped so regions run down the side, months run across the top, average sale sits in every cell, and a Grand Total row and column summarize the whole quarter.

Three regions, three months, two sales recorded for every single region and month combination. Eighteen rows in total, which is already a lot to absorb as a flat list. A pivot table turns it into something you can read in one glance.

code.content:
report = pd.pivot_table(sales, index="region", columns="month", values="sale", aggfunc="mean", margins=True)
report

# month     Feb        Jan        Mar         All
# region
# East    290.0      280.0      270.0       280.0
# North   220.0      220.0      200.0  213.333333
# South   170.0      160.0      150.0       160.0
# All  226.666667    220.0 206.666667  217.777778

blocks.title: Columns land in alphabetical order, not calendar order
blocks.content: pivot_table sorts columns by default, so Jan, Feb, Mar came back as Feb, Jan, Mar instead of chronological order. Pandas has no idea that Jan comes before Feb, it just sees three text strings and sorts them alphabetically. Reindexing the columns yourself fixes the order for the final report.

blocks.text: Read that table for ten seconds and you already know the shape of the quarter. East is comfortably the strongest region every single month. North holds fairly steady around 200 to 220. South trails behind everyone and dips further in March. None of that was easy to see sitting in eighteen separate rows of raw transactions.
And because you now know pivot_table is really groupby underneath, you could reproduce the core grid, minus the convenience of margins, with the same two calls from the previous section.

Notice what you did not have to hand write anywhere in that groupby version: the Grand Total row, the Grand Total column, and the single overall average sitting in the corner. That bookkeeping is exactly what margins=True buys you for free, and it is the main reason pivot_table earns its own function instead of just being a groupby recipe you retype every time.
9. Quick Recap

items: pivot_table reshapes long, row based data into a wide grid, exactly like the pivot tables you have built by hand in a spreadsheet.
index picks the column whose unique values become row labels. columns picks the column whose unique values become column headers.
values picks the column that gets aggregated, and aggfunc picks how, defaulting quietly to mean if you leave it out.
A missing row and column combination shows up as NaN by default. fill_value replaces those gaps with a real number such as 0.
Passing a list to aggfunc, or to values, produces several stacked blocks of columns in the same result.
margins=True adds an All row, an All column, and a grand total cell, all computed from the real underlying data rather than the visible grid.
pivot_table is syntactic sugar over groupby, an aggregation, and unstack. When the grid shape does not fit what you need, groupby directly still works.

blocks.text: pivot_table is the tool you reach for the moment a groupby result needs to look like a report instead of a list. Keep the Excel drag and drop picture in your head, index into Rows, columns into Columns, values into Values, and every parameter in this lesson will keep making sense long after you have forgotten the exact syntax.
